meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means ability .

You have some legs and you need to put them in the trash. But you'll get caught if you put them in one trash can. Quick, cut them up and allocate them to different trash cans around the city. Then you'll never get caught.
See the guy sitting in the box? His head is sticking out of the top. That's a bathtub he's sitting in.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means cheap .
This is the clothes radical, it looks a little like clothes hanging on a clothes hanger, right? Now that these clothes are hung up, you've gotta get to the rest of that pile…
Can you see the flipped $ sign? That's the dollar radical. It was drawn by a kid, so naturally, it's a little backwards, but we won't be the ones to correct the artistic vision!

This is the football radical. Do you see the little footballer with their massive helmet just in the process of kicking the ball away? 100% determination, with zero idea of what's going on. Team Kanji, let's gooo!
This ice is in the shape of a stick. It's an icicle ! You can even see two little ice chunks breaking off of it on the left side.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means peace .
This is the saw radical. Can you see the rectangular hacksaw-style saw in front of that tree trunk that's about to be sawed? I came, I sawed, I conquered.

You use your fingers in the game of football to aid and assist the other players. And when you smash your fingers in football, you need to get some aid yourself. If you're from the UK, just imagine someone kicking or stomping on your fingers instead. Hints Picture yourself playing football. You catch the ball with your fingers and then assist your team by running and smashing your body into the enemy team. But in the process you smash your fingers... so you need to go to the aid tent.
readingMnemonic: When you need aid for your football wrecked fingers you can't help but feel like it's the en d ( えん ) for you. Your fingers hurt so much, you don't even want the nice nurses to aid you. Hints You can't assist your team anymore because you got hurt. This isn't fair! It's the end. The end of your life and your career. Boo hoo hoo!

meaningMnemonic: You have a great ability because your heart gives you the appearance of a superhuman. Your heart is really strong and powerful, fuelling your body to the best of its ability. All this together gives you the appearance of someone in top condition. Hints See yourself in this ideal appearance. Everyone loves to look at you because you look so awesome. Your heart has given you many great abilities. Feel strong and powerful in this body of yours.
readingMnemonic: While you may have the appearance of someone who is super strong, powerful, and awesome, you do have one shortcoming. You don’t know how to tie ( たい ) a tie. Actually, you don’t even know how to tie your shoes, let alone your tie. How embarrassing. Hints Since you don’t know how to tie a tie or tie your shoes, you wear slip ons and clip ons. Hear the noise of Velcro being undone as you kick off your shoes and unclip your tie after a hard day’s work at the office.

meaningMnemonic: They say yoga is the correct way to go through birth . Birth isn't easy, but people keep telling you that yoga is the right way to prepare and actually do it. Hints Picture multiple people you know saying you should do yoga if you plan to give birth. It isn't a question of whether you want to, it's the correct way to do it. So you should.
readingMnemonic: To prepare for giving birth you end up doing so much yoga outside that you get a really deep tan ( たん ). Hints Hopefully having a tan doesn't make birth harder, since you've worked so hard to do this the correct way with so much yoga.

meaningMnemonic: The clothes radical and the clothes kanji are exactly the same! Surprising!
readingMnemonic: An ea gle ( い ) sees a pile of your clothes and lays an e gg ( え ) in them. The eagle’s egg needs a soft warm place to incubate, and your pile of clothes is the perfect place. Hints Look at the eagle and her egg sitting atop your clothes. Every time you get close the eagle starts to screech at you fiercely. Screee! Screee!

meaningMnemonic: See all those icicle s to the dog 's left? Good thing they all fell on his left, or he would've been in a terrible condition . Hints Picture a bunch of big, sharp icicles all falling down directly next to this dog. Now imagine the condition he would've been in, had they all fallen directly on top of him. Poor little thing.
readingMnemonic: What saved the dog's condition was none other than Joe ( じょう ), the local farmhand. He constantly keeps an eye on the dog's condition, including any dangerously sharp icicles that could descend on him. Hints Good guy Joe, always worrying about his dog's condition. Everyone needs a farmhand like Joe.

meaningMnemonic: You use the power of your mouth to spit shellfish at people as a form of congratulations ! In fact, you yell "CONGRATULATIONS!" as the shellfish come pouring out of your powerful mouth. Hints Shellfish were once used as currency, so this totally makes sense. Just think of the shellfish as money coming out of your mouth as you say your congratulations.
readingMnemonic: When you say congratulations like this, you look just like a ga rgoyle ( が ). You're crouching down, your mouth wide open, just like a stone gargoyle. Hints The next time you're congratulating someone, assume the gargoyle stance and dump all of their congratulatory shellfish on them from your mouth.

meaningMnemonic: You use a bamboo saw to cut down tree s to construct and build a building. The bamboo saw was crafted by a master bamboosmith, and cuts through trees with ease so you can quickly construct this new building. Hints Imagine yourself working the bamboo saw. It's made of bamboo, but its sharp edge glistens with a mysterious aura as you slice through tree after tree. Feel how unnaturally easy it is to cut down piles of logs to build with.
readingMnemonic: As you construct and build this building, you hear a strange cheeping noise. Suddenly a chick ( ちく ) pops out of one of the logs you are building with. Then another, and another. You're surrounded by chicks! Is this because you used the magical(?) bamboo saw?? Hints Imagine trying to construct the rest of this building covered in baby chicks. They're very cute, but this is dangerous! You have to build very carefully, so you don't accidentally hurt any of them.

meaningMnemonic: Inside the building is the Winter Cow . You need to see it, so you go inside. It is deep down in there, and you'll have to descend to reach it. Hints Focus on descending the stairs. There are many signs that say "To Winter Cow: descend" with an arrow pointing down. "I guess I'll have to descend," you say.
readingMnemonic: You descend to the bottom and there it is, the Winter Cow. You walk up to the cow, and it swings its head back to see you. Instead of a cow's face, it's こう いち 's face. Hints "Hello, thank you for descending all the way down here to see me," says the Winter Cow with こういち 's face. "You thought you could use the Winter Cow to stop me, but as you can see, I got here first."

meaningMnemonic: You kiss each and every one of your best pals to show them how much you love and care for them. You kiss each friend right on the mouth. Hints Imagine kissing each of your best friends on the mouth. Does this make you uncomfortable? Excited? Both? Feel that feeling.
readingMnemonic: Actually, each and every one of your best pals is of the cock ( かく ) variety. By that, I mean each of them is a rooster. Imagine kissing each cock on its beak. Hints Kissing the cock beak is kind of a strange experience. Feel the feathers in your hands as you steady the cock to kiss it. Cock-a-doodle-doo!

meaningMnemonic: You should say " peace " before you evaluate a situation. That way everyone will know where you’re coming from. If you’re honest and say "peace" before you evaluate a situation out loud, everyone will know where you stand. Hints What situation would you like to evaluate? Be sure to say "peace" before doing so. Imagine yourself doing this out loud and think of what you would say.
readingMnemonic: When you say "peace," you end up making a really bad pun and you hear somebody say “ Heyo !” ( ひょう ) You look at the people around you and try to evaluate who said heyo, but you can’t tell. You start talking again when somebody exclaims “That’s what she said” and another person shouts “Heyo!” once again, but you still can’t evaluate who’s saying these things. Hints Imagine yourself trying to explain a situation you’re about to evaluate and your audience keeps shouting “Heyo!” every other sentence. Imagine how frustrating that would be. Get angry at your rude audience and how much they shout “Heyo.”

meaningMnemonic: Dollar s and shellfish are used to pay expense s and cost s. Shellfish used to be used as currency, so they're like the coins that go with dollars. Hints Imagine opening your bank account and looking at all of your monthly expenses. Now drag the little dollar and shellfish icons over to cover all of those costs.
readingMnemonic: What is the biggest expense and cost ? It's the hea t ( ひ ) bill. Hints When you see how expensive your heat is, you feel a heat going through your body too.

meaningMnemonic: You're always comparing yourself to the next woman because you're obsessed with your figure and appearance . It's not healthy, but when physical form is the only thing that matters to you, comparing yourself to the next woman over becomes a matter of habit. Hints Try to picture this proverbial "next woman." Ugh, her figure is just perfect. And her appearance? So put-together.
readingMnemonic: Plot twist: when you're comparing yourself to the next woman, the figure and appearance you're picturing is actually that of a shee p ( し ). No wonder you're always dissatisfied with your appearance. You're not a sheep, you're a human! Hints Imagine standing in front of the mirror, wishing desperately that you could see the figure of a sheep reflected back at you. What do you have to do to attain that round, fluffy appearance???

meaningMnemonic: The womb is a circle of power where a force of nature is formed. The womb has the power to create life. Life is a force of nature, and the circle of life starts in the womb. Hints Imagine yourself in the womb, the circle of power. You’re being born into the world. Feel the force of your mother all around you.
readingMnemonic: Now pretend you're the mother. You'll need all the force you can muster to bring that baby into the world, so you grab hold of your special sa ber ( せい ) and slice it about in the air to give you the extra force you need. Hints All that force works wonders, and when the baby's born you slice through the umbilical cord with your saber.

meaningMnemonic: You have something to say , so you stand up, throw in the towel , and shout: "I GIVE UP !" The stand radical looks a little weird in this kanji, probably because you're all tired and ready to give up. Hints Imagine standing up and throwing in the towel (or even just waving it around, especially if it's white) — it's the universal signal for giving up, right? Just make sure you also say it out loud, to make it clear for everyone: "I GIVE UP!"
readingMnemonic: What's making you want to give up ? Well, there's a killer ( あきら ) behind you who's threatening to kill you if you don't. Hints Hey, whatever you're doing, it's not worth losing your life over. If a killer is threatening you, you should probably just give up for now and live to fight another day.

meaningMnemonic: You can use a jackhammer to indicate and show someone where the prize is buried. You buried the prize to keep it safe, but the jackhammer is great at unearthing it. Jackhammers do a great job and show where the treasure lies. They indicate quite clearly where one needs to go. Hints Imagine using this jackhammer to show someone where the prize is buried. Feel the vibrations through your hands and the rest of your body.
readingMnemonic: Actually, you're unearthing Je sus ( じ ). He’s the treasure. For your soul. He’s here to show you that Jesus is still a hip and cool guy and he wants to indicate to you that having faith in Jesus and God and stuff is super rad. Jesus is all like, “Who has two thumbs and wants to show you the way of the Lord? This guy.” Hints Picture Jesus getting all over the top and super preachy about his religious beliefs. He’s doing everything he can to indicate to the crowd that he’s the best, and show them how cool he is. Listen to Jesus preach to the crowd, desperate for their attention.

meaningMnemonic: From the roof , an icicle falls and hits Wolverine in the forehead , and he has to go over to the stool to lie down . And eventually he goes to sleep . Hints Picture this entire scene. The icicle falls in slow motion from the roof. It hits wolverine right in the middle of his forehead. He goes down. He has to lie down. He has to sleep.
readingMnemonic: While wolverine sleep s, he makes a horrible neigh ing ( ね ) sound. It's like there's a giant horse in his mouth screaming to get out! NEIGH NEIGH! Hints Wolverine might have a concussion that's making him neigh in his sleep. I guess it's good that he's lying down, but I'm pretty sure you're not supposed to sleep... Maybe you should wake him up so the neighing will stop—I mean, so he'll be okay!

meaningMnemonic: A Viking who knows how to use a bathtub will have to manage all the baths for the other Vikings. Vikings aren't so great with bathing... if you can get one Viking to figure it out he has to manage the rest of them. Hints Picture a Viking trying to manage his Viking friends so they'll use the bathtub properly. He has to manage which people go in when, how hot or cold the water is, and provide all the soap. It's a very important job.
readingMnemonic: The poor Viking trying to manage all the others keeps having to confiscate a corns ( えい ). "You can't take baths in acorns and wood, it has to be water!" he shouts. Hints Some of the Vikings managed to fill their bathtubs with acorns and are trying to rub themselves clean with them instead of water...

meaningMnemonic: Can you look at the dirt and know which direction you need to go? Then you might be a monk . Monks have amazing skills like that. And I'm sure you've seen monks wandering around in lots of media. They don't need maps or smartphones. They just look at the dirt and let the earth guide them to where they need to be. Hints Picture a monk walking through a large field in the middle of nowhere. He knows where to go, he's not afraid. The dirt will lead him in the right direction.
readingMnemonic: You want to know the monk 's trick so you hide behind him for a while as he walks. Finally the monk stops, looks around, takes out a bow ling ( ぼう ) ball and starts bowling in the dirt. The bowling ball rolls off, the monk follows it, and then heads off in that direction. Hints Imagine a monk bowling in the middle of the road. Imagine your shock at how well he handles the ball. Also, imagine how heavy it must be for a monk to carry a bowling ball everywhere!

meaningMnemonic: You'll be put in a net if you try to say things with a knife — that's your penalty . You can't just go up to other people and say things with a knife out. That's why the police have to put you in a net, as a penalty. Hints Imagine getting so mad that you use a knife to say what you're trying to say. A net falls over you and pulls you down. The knife goes flying. This is your penalty for acting like a crazy person.
readingMnemonic: Your penalty for breaking the law isn't over. Now that you're stuck in a net, you can't fight back when they hit you with bats ( ばつ ). Hints If you don't want to be punished with bats, just skip the whole knife thing. Use your words to say what you mean, mmkay?

meaningMnemonic: A cheap tree has a plan . A plan to stay cheap. Hints Picture a tree coming up with some elaborate plans to make sure they can spend as little money as possible.
readingMnemonic: The cheap tree's plan involves only buying an chovies ( あん ) and surviving on them. Good exposure to the sun and fresh water is too expensive. The tree plans to save money by eating anchovies. Hints You're not sure about this anchovy plan. Are you cheap enough to choose a life of eating only anchovies?

meaningMnemonic: With a bamboo tree resting atop your head , you devise a plan . The plan is actually for getting the bamboo tree off of your head. You’re trapped under it. Hints Imagine being trapped under this bamboo tree that is resting on your head. You’re stuck. Feel the weight of the bamboo tree pressing on your head as you try and devise a plan to get out from under it.
readingMnemonic: But why is this bamboo tree so heavy? You look to each end of the bamboo and realize that there is a sack ( さく ) tied on each end. Each sack seems to be filled with heavy rocks. Looks like someone made a plan to trap you here. Now you have to devise a plan to escape! Hints Bamboo is usually kind of light, but this bamboo has a sack of rocks tied to each end making it heavy. Imagine yourself trying to remove this bamboo tree by pushing it up and away from you. It’s like doing a bench-press, bamboo style.

meaningMnemonic: You extend your fingers toward the sun from atop a coat rack because you are about to present your ideas to a crowd. You need to be striking an authoritative pose from an elevated position in order to submit your thoughts persuasively. Hints Extending your fingers upward makes you look like some sort of prophet, and sitting up on the coat rack puts you head and shoulders above all your listeners. Well, go ahead: present your ideas. (You do have something to present, right?)
readingMnemonic: So, what are you going to present to everyone? A slideshow about ta ter tots ( てい ). You made a little PowerPoint to present your personal ranking of the best tater tots you've ever eaten — with photos, of course. Hints At the end of your presentation, you ask everyone to submit a feedback questionnaire, and you present free tater tot samples to everyone who does. What a fun presentation.

meaningMnemonic: You need your net to be straight before you put it on the ground and try to lure something into it. You put your net there to catch something, but if it's twisted or tangled, it won't be very effective. Hints Imagine that some wild animal wanders into your net. Yes! You knew putting the net there was a good idea. But wait… Oh no, it escaped! It turns out your net wasn't straight when you put it there.
readingMnemonic: Then you decide to put chee se ( ち ) in your net. With a perfectly straight net and the cheese you put down as bait, there’s no way this fails. Success is all about how you put the net down and the cheese you put in it. Hints Imagine the smell of the cheese as you put it in the net. Maybe a sharp cheddar? The aroma really carries. All the better to attract more animals! Soon you’ll be putting your cheese-eating prey on the dinner table.

meaningMnemonic: Lying in the dirt , a drunkard puts her mouth to the ground to understand the region . She loves to know all the regional differences among wines and other alcohols, and to her there's no better way to do this than putting her mouth on the ground and literally tasting each region. Hints Picture this drunkard in the dirt, her mouth pressed to the ground. "Ahh," she says, "so this is the taste of the Bordeaux region." Then she has a glass of Bordeaux, and starts noting all its particular regional qualities.
readingMnemonic: Turns out she thinks everything from this region is icky ( いき ). In fact, to the drunkard, every region tastes icky and gross. You don't have the heart to tell her it's the dirt and ground, not the region itself, that tastes icky… Hints Imagine her crying out, "Why are there such icky, earthy notes in all these regional wines?!" Feel the second-hand embarrassment for her. In her drunkenness she can't understand that putting her mouth on the ground makes everything taste icky, no matter what region it's from.

meaningMnemonic: In the ground of the rice paddy is a treasure . As you pull it out of the mucky ground, you can feel your life force being renew ed. Hints Seems like the treasure has some magical ability to renew the cells in your body. Really try to imagine this feeling as you pull the treasure out of the rice paddy’s ground. Perhaps it feels just as refreshing as getting a full night’s sleep.
readingMnemonic: Just as you were getting accustomed to this life renew ing treasure, こう いち comes out of nowhere, stealing your treasure and running off with it. Hints All you could hear was a sly “yoink!”, and suddenly your life renewing treasure was gone. God knows what things こういち will get up to with this life renewing treasure in his possession (but it sure won’t be anything good).

meaningMnemonic: If someone gets under the canopy over your heart you should respond to them. Hints You usually ignore everyone, but this one person... they really got under there and touched your heart. You finally feel like they're the right person to respond to.
readingMnemonic: You respond and it turns out it was to the 王 ( おう ). Hints The 王 touched your heart, you responded, and now you're together. It's like a fairy tale!

meaningMnemonic: It may just be a roof over a bathtub , but this here is actually a Shinto shrine . Hints It is indeed just a roof over a bathtub, but I guess spirits inhabit everything according to Shintoism, so there's no reason this bathtub can't be a Shinto shrine too.
readingMnemonic: What god does this Shinto shrine hold? You see that "It's a- me-ya ( みや )! (Mario!)" Hints It makes sense, the person who says "It's-a-me! (Mario)" is someone who works on bathtubs (and plumbing).

meaningMnemonic: Everyone likes your outfit . The reason ? Your cool sleeve s. You are rocking some absolutely amazing sleeves, and that's reason enough for everyone to love your whole look. Hints Imagine these incredible sleeves you're wearing. Are they flashy and colorful? Puffed and billowing? Jeweled and ornate? Whatever the case, they really bring your outfit together.
readingMnemonic: Little does everyone know, you wear these sleeve s because your arms would be so de ad ( そで ) without them. Why? Because they'd be all exposed and defenseless! Hints Imagine all the ways your arms would be so dead if you didn't have sleeves. Sunburn, bug bites, miscellaneous cuts and scrapes... Just so, so dead. Good thing you've got these stylish, fancy sleeves to protect them.

meaningMnemonic: Your mouth is like an escalator you use to suck and inhale things into your body. Hints If you're ever having trouble remembering how to suck or inhale, just picture an actual escalator that leads into your mouth. That'll definitely help.
readingMnemonic: Use this mouth ability to suck cu cumbers ( きゅう ) into your mouth. Cucumbers are shaped like cylinders so you can suck them into your mouth like this. Just as nature intended. Hints You can inhale a cucumber too, I suppose, but don't tell anyone I told you to.

meaningMnemonic: While riding on your scooter , you grow a mustache on top of the mustache you already have in order to surpass the people around you. You're in a scooter race and your mustache is the only thing keeping you in the lead, but someone else has a mustache too! So you grow another mustache to surpass them once again! Hints Picture yourself running on a scooter with a bunch of other people and closing your eyes tight, willing another mustache to sprout out of your face to surpass them all.
readingMnemonic: Suddenly, something else manages to surpass you all. It's a ca r ( か )! A car with two mustaches is also riding on a scooter and going way faster than you. Hints Watch helplessly as the car surpasses every single one of your scooters. Both of your mustaches droop in shame.

meaningMnemonic: Taking orders from a geoduck will place you into enemy territory . Geoducks make terrible commanders, so if you take orders from one, expect to end up in unknown territory, potentially even enemy territory. Be prepared. Hints Imagine this geoduck shouting orders at you to march into enemy territory. See its gross body as a mouth forms and starts shouting out orders.
readingMnemonic: Not wanting to end up dead in enemy territory , you decide to escape this geoduck leader by getting on a row ( りょう ) boat and rowing your way outta there. The geoduck commander orders you to halt your escape, but you still get in your row boat and row away. Hints Feel yourself in the row boat as you imagine rowing away to safe territory. Hear the geoduck in the background shouting at you from shore, ordering you to return to land.

meaningMnemonic: The light of the moon is shining on a guard who’s been on duty all night. In fact, the moon light is making him so warm, he’s trying to undress and escape ! Somebody stop him! Hints Picture the guard being so warm from the moonlight that he’s trying to simultaneously undress and escape. You can’t just let him leave his post!
readingMnemonic: You’re unable to stop the guard from undress ing and making his escape , so you decide to start throwing some darts ( だつ ) at him. Perhaps that’ll make him stop. Hints Imagine yourself desperately throwing darts at the undressing, escaping guard, trying to make him stop. Or perhaps trying to pin his clothes to his body using the darts. Anything to stop this madness!

meaningMnemonic: You take all of your thread and allocate them into one place to unite them. With all your thread united and wrapped together, you're ready to rule and govern the world! Hints Allocate all of your thread like you would your cash: by uniting it! Not at a bank, but in a big, intertwined lump. Now nobody can stop you and your big lump of thread!
readingMnemonic: You're busy trying to unite all of your thread, twisting and tying and wrapping, and suddenly you look at the ball in your hands and see とう きょう . You've united this thread into the shape of とうきょう . There are even little pins for all the famous neighborhoods and tourist spots. This is strange, because you don't remember putting them there. Hints Try to do this yourself at home. Unite all of your thread and poof! There's とうきょう !

meaningMnemonic: A great leader can look straight at something and know its value . That social media site? 44 billion dollars. That job position? 50k a year. A four-day work week? Um… sorry, no, there's no value there. See? Leaders can see straight to the heart of matters to grasp something's true value. Hints Imagine how terrifying it is when your leader looks straight at YOU. Don't worry, though — you've got more value than you give yourself credit for, and your leader can surely see that.
readingMnemonic: One thing your leader knows has great value is chee se ( ち ). Say goodbye to your days of casually snacking on cheesy treats from the conbini, because your leader's decided the value of cheese is going up 1000%! Hints Imagine the despair you feel walking down the cheese aisle at the store and seeing how one little pack of string cheese now costs the same as your monthly rent. Why did your leader have to spike the value of cheese like this?

meaningMnemonic: The leader only uses the helicopter with the highest value . They choose to fly in only the very best, most valuable helicopter. That's why it's worth way more than the others. Actually, any helicopter they use goes up in value. That's the amazing effect of a good leader. Hints Can you understand the value of this helicopter? The leader flew it to war and back! So of course it's worth a lot!
readingMnemonic: To further increase the helicopter's value , the leader tied it to a ca r ( か ). Wow, now it has the value of a helicopter and a car combined! For a total value of… Well, imagine for yourself what value the car adds. Hints Imagine driving a valuable car with the leader's helicopter on top. Yeah!

meaningMnemonic: That scarecrow with the knife is the vice president. Yeah, I know how he looks, and I'm pretty sure he does some murdering on the side , but you didn't hear that from me. Hints I don't know how we managed to get a knife-wielding scarecrow as a vice president, there's a side of politics I don't get, I guess. I mean, just look at him up there. If something happens to our president we're stuck with that thing.
readingMnemonic: It's the vice president's turn to speak at the podium and he just clears his throat and yells, " F**k ( ふく ) you!" to the crowd, holding up his knife. They cheer. Hints What's going on? Normally if a vice president yells f**k you there would be... I dunno... consequences? What's happening?!

meaningMnemonic: There's an arrow in a turkey that you can see in your view . The turkey seems to be viewing you too, from afar. Hints View the turkey as the turkey views you. View the arrow stuck in it too.
readingMnemonic: As you view the turkey, Genghis Khan ( かん ) suddenly comes into your view too. He towers over the injured turkey, leans down, and... pulls the arrow out!? Hints As you view this strange scene, Genghis Khan turns and views you viewing him. He points two fingers to his eyes and then to you, and marches off into the woods. You also view the turkey running off in the other direction.

meaningMnemonic: The only flowers that the moon gladiator s will water are wisteria . Hints The moon gladiators have a thing for wisterias.
readingMnemonic: Since they're on the moon, where did they get the wisteria from? Actually, from one of the points on earth that is nearest to the moon, Mt. Fuji ( ふじ ). Hints Imagine them reaching down from the moon and plucking some wisteria up from Mt. Fuji then taking them back up to the moon. Now they water them.

meaningMnemonic: This is like your side part of speech , as in, you add it to the side of a verb because it's an adverb .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私は昨日、日本語の時を表す副詞を学びました。
sentences.english: I learned Japanese adverbs that show time yesterday.

sentences.japanese: その副詞の使い方がよく分からないので、今辞書で調べているところなんです。
sentences.english: I'm not sure how to use that adverb, so I'm looking it up in the dictionary right now.

sentences.japanese: 副詞節と名詞節の違いを説明しなさい。
sentences.english: Explain the difference between an adverbial clause and a noun clause.

meaningMnemonic: Penalty gold is the money you pay when you get a penalty. It's for a fine .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ばつ gets changed to ばっ though, so don't get it wrong (or you'll get a 罰金 !).

sentences.japanese: 罰金については、また追って連絡します。
sentences.english: We’ll contact you shortly about the fine.

sentences.japanese: 運転中にスマホをチラ見したところを警察に見られて、六千円の罰金を取られた。
sentences.english: The police saw me glancing at my phone while driving and gave me a 6,000 yen fine.

sentences.japanese: 遅刻した社員に罰金を払わせようという提案がありました。

So now when you've tried really hard on something, but you have to abandon it anyway, you shout AKIRA into the sky. I just did it while trying to write this mnemonic!

sentences.japanese: 死んでも漢字の勉強を諦めないで！
sentences.english: Even if you die, don't give up on learning kanji!

sentences.japanese: コウイチはついにポケモンマスターになる夢を諦めた。
sentences.english: Koichi finally abandoned his dream of becoming a Pokemon master.

sentences.japanese: 山のようなレビューを諦めずにやるかリセットするかは、とても難しい選択です。
sentences.english: Doing a mountain of reviews without giving up or resetting—it's a difficult choice.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 手洗い is "handwashing" (and also a not as polite way to mention a bathroom). When you add お you're suddenly making it polite. Why? Because you're talking about something a little more crass than handwashing. You're talking about the toilet or restroom or bathroom . Ewww. Poop goes there.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 手洗い , so if you know that you'll know this too!

sentences.japanese: お手洗いは、真っすぐ行って左です。
sentences.english: The restroom is straight and to the left.

sentences.japanese: ジェームスはいつも、お手洗いに行く前にウィスキーを一口飲む。
sentences.english: James always takes a sip of whiskey before going to the bathroom.

sentences.japanese: お手洗いで用を足しているうちに、座ったまま寝てしまいました。
sentences.english: I dozed off while sitting in the bathroom doing my business.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means indicate so the verb vocab version is to indicate or to show . This is used in contexts like "a study shows that learning Japanese is fun" and "I demonstrated my willingness to learn kanji".
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Studies seem to indicate and to show that shee p me n ( しめ ) are better than regular men in every way. The sheep/man combo is a powerful thing. Or so studies indicate.

sentences.japanese: このマークは何を示しているんですか？
sentences.english: What does this mark indicate?

sentences.japanese: 約束なんてしないで。言葉ではなく行いで示してよ。
sentences.english: Don’t promise me anything. Actions speak louder than words.

sentences.japanese: ここに名前とメールアドレスを入力すると、自分の就職市場における価値が示されるらしいよ。
sentences.english: Apparently, if you enter your name and email address here, it will show you your value in the job market.

meaningMnemonic: 判断 is judgement. Make that into a verb and you have to judge , or to conclude .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 判断 before learning this, but if you don't I won't judge you (the Crabigator will).

sentences.japanese: 食用キノコか毒キノコかを判断するのは難しい。
sentences.english: It's difficult to judge whether it's an edible or poisonous mushroom.

sentences.japanese: よく人を見た目で判断してはいけないと言いますが、それは本当に正しいことだと思いますか？
sentences.english: It's often said you shouldn't judge people by their appearance, but do you think that's really true?

sentences.japanese: これまでに聞いたことから判断すると、どうやら真打ちは最後にあるようだね。
sentences.english: Judging from what I've heard, the best seems to have been saved for last.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 飛ぶ is to fly? Well this word is for when you make some thing fly. So, this word is to let something fly or to send something flying . It also means to skip over something , such as someone's turn or a question on a test.
readingMnemonic: The reading is just like 飛ぶ , so if you know that reading you're close. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember the second part: You can use your strength to let something fly , and that something is a bus ( ばす ). You're that buff!

sentences.japanese: 僕の順番を飛ばさないでよ！
sentences.english: Don't skip over my turn!

sentences.japanese: コウイチがつまらない冗談を飛ばすと、ビエトは不機嫌になる。
sentences.english: When Koichi cracks a boring joke, Viet gets grumpy.

sentences.japanese: フグは、センターオーバーの三塁打をかっ飛ばした。
sentences.english: Fugu sent a triple flying over center field.

meaningMnemonic: Like with 確か , which means certain , this is the verb version of that. So when you "do certain" you are going to make sure of something or you're going to verify something.
readingMnemonic: This one is kun'yomi followed by okurigana. If you remember the reading you learned with 確かに , you should know this one!

sentences.japanese: ちゃんとドアにカギをかけたかどうか確かめた方がいいですよ。
sentences.english: You should make sure the door is properly locked.

sentences.japanese: アルコール分がちゃんと飛んだかどうか、確かめてくださいね。
sentences.english: Verify that the alcohol content has been completely removed.

sentences.japanese: いつも、カナエさんが単語の使い方に間違いが無いか、辞書で確かめてくれています。
sentences.english: Kanae always checks the dictionary to make sure there are no mistakes in word use.

meaningMnemonic: The pressure used easily collapse s whatever it's pushing against. That's why this verb means to overwhelm .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that the あつ goes to あっ , as you'd probably expect.

sentences.japanese: ダリンは自然の美しさに圧倒された。
sentences.english: Darin was overwhelmed by the beauty of the nature.

sentences.japanese: この新しいサイトは他社の日本語学習サイトを圧倒するだろう。
sentences.english: This new site will overwhelm other Japanese language sites.

sentences.japanese: ケリー氏は今回の選挙で圧倒的に勝利を収めましたね。彼の勢いには本当に圧倒されました。
sentences.english: Mr. Kerry won this election hands down, didn't he? I was truly astonished by his momentum.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means surpass , but this verb is intransitive, meaning we’re not focussing on who did the action, but on the action itself. So this means to pass , as in “the storm passed”, to be over as in “winter’s over”, or to be too much .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: In order for the storm to pass you’re going to have to sue ( す ) it. Sadly storms won’t pass unless you take legal action these days.

sentences.japanese: 夏が過ぎ、木の葉が色づき初めていた。
sentences.english: Summer was over and the leaves on the trees were beginning to change color.

sentences.japanese: トーフグの社員達はみんな、台風が過ぎるのをオフィスで待った。
sentences.english: All the Tofugu employees waited at the office for the typhoon to pass.

sentences.japanese: 昨晩は、晩ご飯を食べ過ぎて、どうしても寝られませんでした。
sentences.english: I couldn't get to sleep last night because I ate too much supper.

meaningMnemonic: You know how 経 means passage of time , right? Well, this is the verb form of that. What does time do when it passages? It passes. So, this verb means to pass or to elapse .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What do you say to time as it begins to pass you by? " Ta ta ( た ), Time!"

sentences.japanese: 一ヶ月が経つ
sentences.english: one month passes

sentences.japanese: 時が経つ
sentences.english: time passes

sentences.japanese: 三年が経つ
sentences.english: three years pass

sentences.japanese: 時間が経つ
sentences.english: time passes

sentences.japanese: 時が経つのを忘れて熱中していました。
sentences.english: I was so engrossed that I lost track of time.

sentences.japanese: あなたがワニカニを始めてから、もう何年経ちましたか？
sentences.english: How many years has it been since you started using WaniKani?

sentences.japanese: 時間が経てばわかるよ。
sentences.english: Time will tell.

sentences.japanese: 急に片目が全く見えなくなったら、できるだけ早く目医者さんに行ってください。時間が経てば経つほど、治すのが難しくなる可能性があります。
sentences.english: If one eye suddenly becomes completely blind, please go to an eye doctor as soon as possible. The longer you wait, the more difficult it may be to treat.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. This is an intransitive verb, meaning that the piercing just happens, without emphasis on what makes it happen. That's why it means to pierce into , to stick in , or to stab into . This is a tricky word because its English translations often end up being transitive, but in Japanese we always use this with the particle に , not を , so it's intransitive. You can see this in phrases like 言葉が心に刺さった (the words pierced my heart).
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 刺す .

sentences.japanese: 言葉が刺さる
sentences.english: words strike a chord in one's heart

sentences.japanese: トゲが刺さる
sentences.english: a thorn sticks into something

sentences.japanese: 矢が刺さる
sentences.english: an arrow pierces into something

sentences.english: a needle sticks into something

sentences.japanese: 目に刺さる
sentences.english: something pierces the eye

sentences.japanese: 喉に刺さる
sentences.english: something pierces the throat, something gets stuck in one's throat

sentences.japanese: 胸に刺さる
sentences.english: something goes straight to the heart, something pierces the chest

sentences.japanese: 心に刺さる
sentences.english: something goes straight to the heart

sentences.japanese: それは心に刺さる言葉だった。
sentences.english: They were words that struck a chord in my heart.

sentences.japanese: 矢が頭に刺さった。
sentences.english: An arrow embedded itself in his head.

sentences.japanese: トゲが刺さらないように気をつけてね。
sentences.english: Be careful not to get pricked by a thorn.

meaningMnemonic: When you do a penalty to someone you are trying to punish or to penalize them.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Just remember that the つ becomes a small っ so I don't have to punish you.

sentences.japanese: その選手は明らかにドーピングをしていたのに、罰せられなかったんだ。
sentences.english: The athlete was clearly doping, yet he wasn't punished.

sentences.japanese: ウソをついている子どもがいたら、罰する前にまず理由を聞いてあげるべきです。
sentences.english: If a child is lying, you should first ask why before punishing them.

sentences.japanese: コウイチはトーフグの秘密を漏らした従業員を罰した。
sentences.english: Koichi punished the employees who leaked Tofugu’s secrets.

meaningMnemonic: When you put something you don't just put it, you have to put down this item or even (to) set down the item. Basically, you have to put something down with this verb. It's a little different from the kanji meaning you learned but not that different.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Just imagine you're putting down O reos ( お ). One after another. Each oreo that you try to put down say in your head "Hello Mr. Oreo, I'm going to put you down.. ooh yes, you like that don't you?" REPEAT.

sentences.japanese: 赤ん坊をベビーベッドに置くことに成功した。
sentences.english: I successfully placed the baby in the crib.

sentences.japanese: ギョウザの皮の中央に具材を置いてください。
sentences.english: Place the ingredients in the center of the gyoza skin.

sentences.japanese: フグと私は今距離を置いてるの。
sentences.english: Fugu and I are putting some distance between us right now.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means cover , so the verb version means to put on , to wear , or to cover oneself with . 被る is used when you wear things that cover your head or face, like hats, helmets, and masks, or when cover yourself with something, like pulling a blanket over yourself. Figuratively, it can also refer to overlapping events — think of it like one event "covering" another on a timeline. Since the kanji's other meaning is incur , 被る can also mean taking on a burden or blame — incurring responsibility, in other words.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Every time you go to put on your hat, you yell " KABOO M ( かぶ )!" Why? Because your hat is da bomb. Go ahead, try it: put on your super cool hat while shouting out "KABOOM!" Is everyone looking at you now? Did they realize the hat you're wearing is da bomb?

sentences.japanese: この仕事では、安全のためにヘルメットを被る必要があります。
sentences.english: In this job, it's necessary to wear a helmet for safety.

sentences.japanese: この写真でニューヨーク・ヤンキースのキャップを被ってるのが私の弟です。
sentences.english: In this photo, the one wearing the New York Yankees cap is my brother.

sentences.japanese: うちの子は、他人の前ではいつも猫を被ります。
sentences.english: My child always wears a mask of innocence in front of non-family members.

sentences.japanese: ストッキングを被った男が銀行からお金を持って走って出ていくのを見ました。銀行に入るタイミングが被らなくて良かった！
sentences.english: I saw a man wearing pantyhose over his head running out of the bank with money. I'm glad our timing for entering the bank didn't coincide!

meaningMnemonic: If 在留 is residence , then the verb version of that would be to reside . Like 在留 , this is also a more formal term. You might encounter it at the immigration office, but you probably won't hear it in everyday conversation.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 在留 so you should be able to read this one already!

sentences.japanese: 外国人が日本に在留する時に必要になるものは何ですか？
sentences.english: What do foreigners need when they stay in Japan?

sentences.japanese: もちろん、私は在留資格を持って、日本に在留しています。
sentences.english: Of course, I am residing in Japan with residence status.

sentences.japanese: 私がこの国に在留することができる期間は限られているんです。
sentences.english: I have a limited amount of time to stay in this country.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means respond so the verb vocab version is to respond . 応じる is a formal word that describes acting favorably in response to a call, request, or demand. For example, 注文に応じる goes beyond just taking orders; it means adapting appropriately and fulfilling them.
readingMnemonic: The reading is actually the same as the one you learned with the kanji! Not too shabby.

sentences.japanese: ジョンはゼッタイに説得には応じないつもりみたいだよ。
sentences.english: John seems absolutely determined not to be persuaded.

sentences.japanese: ニコラス・ケイジは、サインがほしいというファンの申し出に、笑顔で応じた。
sentences.english: Nicolas Cage responded with a smile to a fan's request for an autograph.

sentences.japanese: 先方は、我々の二割りの値下げ要求に応じるでしょうか？
sentences.english: Do you think they will accept our request for a 20% discount?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means manage , but when you manage something, what are you usually managing? How about a business? So this word means to run a business even though the kanji is manage.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You run a business called Eat O'Na chos ( いとな ). It's your classic run-of-the-mill Mexican-Irish joint (hence the name). Delicious nachos served with Irish flair.

sentences.japanese: 私のおじは、岡山県でイタリアン・レストランを営んでいます。
sentences.english: My uncle runs an Italian restaurant in Okayama prefecture.

sentences.japanese: コウイチは、事業を営む天才だ。
sentences.english: Koichi is a genius at managing a business.

sentences.japanese: 私の両親はマッサージ業を営んでいるので、私はそこで「マッサージ受け放題」なんです。
sentences.english: My parents run a massage therapy business, so I can get 'all-you-can-take-massages' there.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means earthquake so the verb means to shiver and to shake , like you would if there was an earthquake happening right now.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You start to shake in an earthquake because you're really full ( ふる ) from eating lunch. Now your full belly is shaking and quaking with the ground! Ahh it's awful! You never want to be full again!

sentences.japanese: アル中の父の手は、いつも震えていた。
sentences.english: My alcoholic father's hands were always shaking.

sentences.japanese: すごく価値のある絵をフリーマーケットで見つけた時、全身が震えました。
sentences.english: When I found a painting of great value at a flea market, I trembled.

sentences.japanese: 寒さで震えている子犬を見ると、涙が止まらなくなりました。
sentences.english: I couldn't stop crying when I saw a puppy shivering from the cold.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means sleep or lie down , so the verb vocab version is to sleep or to lie down —just like what you do when you decide to go to bed .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. So, you can go ahead and lie down for a moment before moving on to the next item.

sentences.japanese: よし、そろそろ寝るね〜。おやすみ〜。また明日〜。
sentences.english: Alright, I'm gonna go to bed. Sleep well. See you in the morning.

sentences.japanese: おやすみ、ダーリン<3 ぐっすり寝てね。
sentences.english: Good night, darling <3 Sleep tight.

sentences.japanese: 日曜日にトーフグのオフィスに行くと、コウイチが床の上で寝ていたことがあった。
sentences.english: I once went to Tofugu's office on a Sunday to find Koichi sleeping on the floor.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means suck so the verb vocab version is to suck , but it's usually used to talk about what you do to cigarettes, so a better translation I think is to smoke .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You smoke too much, and that gives you cancer. You decide to sue ( す ) the cigarette makers.

sentences.japanese: これを最後に、きっぱりとタバコを吸うのを止めるつもりなんだ。
sentences.english: After this one, I’m going to quit smoking once and for all.

sentences.japanese: 生まれたての赤ちゃんは、上手におっぱいが吸えないことも多い。
sentences.english: Newborns frequently struggle to latch on to their mothers’ nipples (to breastfeed).

sentences.japanese: 鼻から息を吸い込んで、口からゆっくり出してください。鼻から息を吸うと、記憶と気分を司る脳の領域が刺激されるんですよ。
sentences.english: Breathe in through your nose and out slowly through your mouth. When you breathe in through your nose, you stimulate the area of your brain that controls memory and mood.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means view so what is the verb vocab version? It's to view or to watch .
readingMnemonic: The reading here is actually the same as 見る . This is easy to remember because the meanings are so similar too, not to mention it has a 見 right inside the kanji itself!

sentences.japanese: その試合を観た時は、確か二十才を過ぎていたと思います。
sentences.english: I think I was over 20 years old when I watched that match.

sentences.japanese: 今日は東京タワーを観に行ってきました。
sentences.english: We went to see Tokyo Tower today.

sentences.japanese: どっちの映画を観るか迷っています。
sentences.english: I can’t decide which movie to watch.

meaningMnemonic: When you transmit something that unite s the people, you are probably pulling on tradition . Tradition is what unites us all and transmits who we are to everyone else. What is your 伝統 ? 伝統 means "tradition" in the sense of customs, practices, or rituals that are passed down within a culture or community. These traditions bring people together across generations and keep our shared culture alive.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: タイラーが飲んでいるのは、アイルランドの伝統のビールです。
sentences.english: What Tyler is drinking is a traditional Irish beer.

sentences.japanese: 北米では、感謝祭の日に七面鳥を食べる伝統があります。
sentences.english: In North America, there is a tradition of eating turkey on Thanksgiving.

sentences.japanese: あの日本の伝統衣装の名前って何だっけ？単語をすっかり忘れちゃったよ。
sentences.english: What was the name of that traditional Japanese costume again? I completely forget the word.

meaningMnemonic: Something is a trouble ( 面倒 ) and it is smelly ( 臭い ). So what is something that's smelly and a trouble? Well, something that's troublesome or a bother , I suppose. Basically you can ignore the smelly part. For some reason someone threw that back in, but smelly things are a bother, I suppose.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the words 面倒 plus 臭い added together, so it is めんどうくさい ! Although the proper reading is めんどうくさい , be aware that people often just say めんどくさい when speaking. That extra う is just such a bother, you know?

sentences.japanese: 毎日シャワーするのって、本当に面倒臭い。
sentences.english: Taking a shower every day is such a bother.

sentences.japanese: 人のグチを聞くことほど面倒臭いことは無い。
sentences.english: There's nothing more annoying than listening to people complain.

sentences.japanese: 白髪が出てきちゃったんだけど、白髪染めをするのは面倒臭いんだよね。
sentences.english: I've started going gray, but it's too much bother to color it.

meaningMnemonic: If you undress from clothes you are undressing . 脱衣 is a relatively formal word that you'll mostly see on the signage for changing rooms at public baths, where they'll be called 脱衣所 or 脱衣場 .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 脱衣をする
sentences.english: to undress

sentences.japanese: 脱衣室
sentences.english: changing room

sentences.japanese: 脱衣場
sentences.english: changing area

sentences.japanese: 脱衣所
sentences.english: changing room

sentences.japanese: 脱衣をしてから入浴してください。
sentences.english: Please undress before taking a bath.

sentences.japanese: 脱衣所にアップルウォッチを忘れてしまいました。
sentences.english: I forgot my Apple Watch in the changing room.

sentences.japanese: 車イスで母を風呂場のドアの前まで運び、脱衣を手伝いました。
sentences.english: I used a wheelchair to take my mother to the bathroom door, then helped her undress.

meaningMnemonic: Something that happens outside the plan is something that happens unexpectedly .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 日本語学習は私にはかなりハードルが高いんじゃないかと思っていたんですが、案外そうでもなかったです。
sentences.english: I thought learning Japanese would be very difficult for me, but unexpectedly, it actually wasn’t that bad.

sentences.japanese: 日本人の魚好きの人でも、魚の小骨が苦手な人って案外多いんですよ。
sentences.english: Even among Japanese fish-lovers, there are a surprisingly large number of people who dislike small fish bones.

sentences.japanese: ご両親、全然そうは見えませんけど、案外お年を召してらっしゃるんですね。
sentences.english: Although they don't look it, your parents are older than I expected.

meaningMnemonic: When you unite and join things together, you get unification ! This can also mean integration and consolidation , which are essentially other ways to describe things being united.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Unify them.

sentences.japanese: この教科書は、色々な学習教材を統合したものです。
sentences.english: This textbook is an integration of various learning materials.

sentences.japanese: データを統合したいんだけど、やり方知ってる？
sentences.english: I want to consolidate the data. Do you know how to do that?

sentences.japanese: 全ての国が一つの政府に統合される日がいつかやってくると思いますか。
sentences.english: Do you think the day will one day come when all countries are united under one government?

meaningMnemonic: Bad feeling s that you dislike are unpleasant feelings . These unpleasant feelings include things like hatred, disgust, revulsion, and fear. All of those are considered to be a part of the term unpleasant feelings.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned these readings already so you should be able to read this one too!

sentences.japanese: 知らない人から急に頭に手を置かれたら、そりゃあ嫌悪感を感じるでしょう。
sentences.english: If a stranger suddenly put his hand on your head, you would surely feel disgusted.

sentences.japanese: それ以来、藤づるを見ると、どうしても嫌悪感にかられるんです。
sentences.english: Since then, whenever I see wisteria vines, I can't help feeling disgusted.

sentences.japanese: あなたと話していると、いつも嫌悪感を抱くんです。
sentences.english: I’m always filled with disgust when I talk with you.

meaningMnemonic: A value and a value . Obviously this is something that has much value .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: コンピュータの無い人生なんて生きてる価値がない。
sentences.english: A life without computers isn’t worth living.

sentences.japanese: そのお皿の価値を知っていますか？
sentences.english: Do you know how much that dish is worth?

sentences.japanese: 多くの人が、トーフグのブログ記事に文学的価値を見出しました。
sentences.english: A lot of people have found literary merit in Tofugu's blog articles.

meaningMnemonic: A value is a value , but only in the mathematical sense. Depending on the reading, this can also mean price .
readingMnemonic: Imagine a numerical value written on a tie ( あたい ). Now imagine that it's the price of a ne igh ( ね ) from your favorite horse. It's a pretty high price, but you'll do anything to hear that horse neigh. Generally, あたい refers to a numerical value in math, while ね is a formal word for "price."

sentences.english: Find the value of x and y.

sentences.japanese: 羽毛布団はやっぱり値が張るね。
sentences.english: A down quilt is expensive, as I expected.

readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned! Now you just have to make sure you know what a Wisteria is... This word is often found in names, like a lot, so look out for it in that way.

sentences.japanese: メニューにある、この藤セットって何ですか？

sentences.japanese: 藤棚には、美しい藤の花が咲いていました。
sentences.english: Beautiful wisteria flowers were blooming on the trellis.

meaningMnemonic: When there's a district in a region , it's called a zone or district . 区域 is a formal word for a kind of designated area , usually one defined by specific boundaries or characteristics. It's often used in urban planning, like for no-parking zones or residential areas. It can also apply to regions like postal districts, police jurisdictions, or restricted areas.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: この区域の治安を良くする方法について、何か提案はありませんか？
sentences.english: Do you have any suggestions on how to improve public safety in this district?
